content: Evaluation, as defined by the United Nations Evaluation Group (UNEG), is a systematic and impartial assessment of an activity, project, program, strategy, policy, theme, sector, operational area, or institutional performance. It examines both expected and achieved accomplishments, focusing on the results chain, processes, contextual factors, and causal links to understand the extent of achievements or the reasons for their absence. The purpose of evaluation is to determine the relevance, impact, effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability of interventions and contributions, particularly those of UN system organizations. The Country Cooperation Strategy (CCS) evaluation aims to assess WHO’s contribution to and influence on the national health development agenda, as aligned with the agreed joint strategic priorities outlined in the CCS. This evaluation is a structured, decentralized process conducted across all three levels of the organization. Its primary objective is to evaluate the effectiveness, efficiency, and quality of WHO’s work in improving health outcomes in a specific country. Additionally, it informs the development of new CCS iterations. CCS evaluation is distinct from other supervisory functions, such as audits or internal control frameworks, which focus on compliance. Instead, CCS evaluation emphasizes results, seeking to understand and document what works, why, and how. It also differs from program budget monitoring and performance assessment by examining broader issues of relevance, context, causality, impact, and sustainability. The evaluation process adheres to WHO’s five key principles: impartiality, independence, utility, quality, and transparency. It is also guided by overarching principles, including a human rights-based approach, gender mainstreaming, and equity in health. The evaluation generates recommendations to influence policy, management, and operational decisions at the country level. The specific objectives of CCS evaluation include: 1. Reviewing the progress, processes, outputs, and outcomes of CCS priorities. 2. Examining the alignment of CCS priorities with the government’s health agenda. 3. Determining the impact of WHO’s work under the current CCS on the country’s health outcomes. 4. Analyzing the harmonization of WHO’s work with other UN agencies through the UNSDCF. 5. Identifying lessons learned from the current CCS to inform the development of the next CCS. The evaluation methodology employs a hybrid approach, including desk reviews, stakeholder interviews, and participatory methods. Evaluation questions are designed to assess the logic of the CCS theory of change and the credibility of its results framework. Data collection involves qualitative and quantitative methods, such as document reviews, interviews, focus group discussions, and feedback sessions with key stakeholders. The evaluation process is participatory, engaging national health authorities, UN system organizations, bilateral development partners, academia, and civil society organizations. Stakeholder involvement is sought throughout the process, from report inception to validation. The evaluation team is composed of individuals with leadership, technical expertise, and experience in evaluation methodologies, ensuring credibility and impartiality. The evaluation report provides clear answers to the evaluation questions, supported by evidence, and includes conclusions, lessons learned, and recommendations for the next CCS. It is shared with senior management at the regional and headquarters levels and disseminated to stakeholders involved in the evaluation process. The report may also be discussed at regional and global management forums and governing body meetings. The evaluation budget is included in the country biennial work plan or respective WHO regional budgets. Additional guidance and resources, such as the WHO Evaluation Practice Handbook, are available to support the evaluation process. The evaluation team follows a structured timeline, from the development of terms of reference to the dissemination of findings, ensuring alignment with WHO’s evaluation policy and quality standards.
